name: Noopept (Omberacetam)
lead: Noopept, also called omberacetam or GVS-111, is a synthetic dipeptide-like compound promoted as a nootropic (cognitive enhancer). Chemically it is N-phenylacetyl-L-prolylglycine ethyl ester, and it is described as a prodrug of the endogenous dipeptide cycloprolylglycine; it is related to the racetam family. It was developed by Russian pharmacology researchers, including T. A. Gudasheva and S. B. Seredenin, and its synthesis was first reported in 1996.[1]

It is registered as a medicine in Russia, while in the United States it is an unapproved "new drug" that the FDA has treated as a piracetam analog, and it is nonetheless sold online as a supplement.[1] Its interest in looksmaxxing-adjacent communities is as a "mental" or recovery compound rather than as an appearance treatment; no source examined links it to any change in physical appearance.

Published work consists mostly of laboratory and animal studies of neuroprotection, plus a small number of Russian clinical comparisons with piracetam. Human evidence is limited, and Wikipedia notes that no long-term studies of chronic use exist.[1][2]
infobox: Medicine in Russia; Schedule 4 in Australia; unapproved new drug in the US[1]

paras: Proposed mechanisms, mostly from rat and cell studies, include antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, limiting calcium- and glutamate-mediated neurotoxicity, and effects on blood rheology.[1] Rodent studies reported increased expression of the growth factors NGF and BDNF in the hippocampus.[3] The metabolite cycloprolylglycine is described as an AMPA receptor modulator that raises BDNF in cell culture.[1] As of 2017, its metabolism and elimination half-life in humans were not well characterised.[1]

Few human studies have been conducted; the longest lasted 56 days.[1] A Russian study compared noopept with piracetam in patients with mild cognitive disorders due to vascular and traumatic brain disease.[4] No long-term studies of chronic use have been published, and no study has examined appearance outcomes.[1]

Laboratory and animal research includes protection of cultured human cortical neurons from oxidative damage,[5] improved spatial memory in a mouse model of Alzheimer-like changes,[2] and effects on diabetes-related parameters in rats.[6]

Legal treatment varies: it is prescription-only (Schedule 4) in Australia, controlled as a psychoactive substance in Hungary since 2020, and available without prescription in Russia. In the United Kingdom, sale for human consumption is prohibited under the Psychoactive Substances Act 2016.[1] Wikipedia reports that the FDA has issued import alerts for it.[1]

timeline.event: Synthesis first reported by Russian researchers.[1]

lore.intro: Noopept appears on looksmax.org mainly in personal discussion of mood and thinking while taking nootropics; the available threads concern mental state rather than appearance.

claims.believers: Users of nootropics describe it as a cognitive aid and discuss it alongside creatine and exercise.
claims.experts: Evidence in humans is limited to small, mostly Russian comparisons with piracetam; no long-term studies exist.[1][4]

claims.believers: Proponents cite laboratory papers on neuron protection.
claims.experts: Neuroprotective effects have been reported in cell and animal models;[2][5] no human trial has established them.

card.summary: A Russian-developed racetam-like nootropic with small human studies and no appearance evidence.
card.note: Unapproved drug in the US; long-term human safety data are lacking.

quick.overview:
Noopept is a synthetic nootropic developed in Russia and sold online as a supplement in many countries. It is chemically related to the racetams.

It is discussed in these communities as a mental-performance compound; no source links it to changes in appearance.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory studies suggest antioxidant effects, reduced excitotoxicity and raised growth factors such as BDNF in rodents. Human mechanisms are not well characterised.
quick.risks: Long-term human safety studies have not been published. It is an unapproved new drug in the US, prescription-only in Australia and registered as a medicine in Russia.
